questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at the Moment When Its Acceleration is Zero
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=(t+1){e}^{-t},\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((t+1){e}^{-t}) \\  & =-t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t{e}^{-t}) \\  & =(t-1){e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =(t-1){e}^{-t} \\ t-1 & =0 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t=1.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
v(1)=-1\cdot {e}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{e}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Intervals of Increasing or Decreasing Displacement
questions.problem: The displacement $s,$ in meters, relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t)=\sqrt{t}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡t,$ where $t>0$ is the time measured in seconds. Determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of decreasing $x,$ then its velocity is negative. 

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡t) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{2\sqrt{t}}+\frac{\sqrt{t}}{t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{2\sqrt{t}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2}{2\sqrt{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x$, we solve the inequality $v(t)<0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & <0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2}{2\sqrt{t}} & <0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t+2 & <0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t & <-2 \\ t & <{e}^{-2} \\ t & <\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of decreasing $x$ is $t\in (0,\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}).$

evidence.solution_quote: Therefore, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of decreasing $x$ is $t\in (0,\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}).$

Determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of decreasing $x,$ then its velocity is negative. 

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t{e}^{-t}) \\  & ={e}^{-t}-t{e}^{-t} \\  & =(1-t){e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x$, we solve the inequality $v(t)<0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & <0 \\ (1-t){e}^{-t} & <0 \\ 1-t & <0 \\ t & >1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of decreasing $x$ is $t\in (1,\infty ).$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at the Moment When Its Acceleration is Zero
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=7{t}^{2}-{t}^{3},\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}) \\  & =14t-3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(14t-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =14-6t\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}14-6t & =0 \\ -6t & =-14 \\ t & =\frac{7}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the acceleration is zero when $t=\frac{7}{3}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{7}{3}) & =14(\frac{7}{3})-3{(\frac{7}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{98}{3}-\frac{49}{3} \\  & =\frac{49}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at the Moment When Its Acceleration is Zero
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)-{t}^{2},\,t>0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.

The acceleration is zero at $t=$
{{field-1}}, and the velocity at this moment is
$v=$
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)-{t}^{2}) \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+t\cdot \frac{1}{t}-2t \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+1-2t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+1-2t) \\  & =\frac{1}{t}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a(t)=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{t}-2 & =0 \\ \frac{1}{t} & =2 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t=\frac{1}{2}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v\,(\frac{1}{2}) & =ln\,(\frac{1}{2})+1-2\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =ln\,(\frac{1}{2})+1-1 \\  & =ln\,(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the acceleration is zero at $t=\frac{1}{2},$ and the velocity at this moment is $v=-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$
